etymology: From the Saxon naedre, a serpent, the initial n lost by wearing into the article (a naddre becoming an adder); in the Authorized Version it renders several Hebrew words for the venomous snake — shephiphon, the horned viper of the path (Gen 49:17); pethen, the deaf asp of Psa 58:4; 'akshub, the swelling adder of Psa 140:3; and tsiph'oni, the biting adder of Pro 23:32.
biblical_def: The adder is the venomous serpent of the Authorized Version, the small death that lies in the road. Jacob’s blessing on Dan sets it in the dust of the path, a serpent by the way that bites the horse heels so that the rider falls backward (Gen 49:17) — a picture of a small enemy bringing down a great one from below. Solomon lays it at the bottom of the wine cup: what goes down smooth and red “at the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder” (Pro 23:32). But the adder’s greatest doctrinal weight lies in Psa 58:4, where the wicked are “like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.” That is total depravity drawn to the life. The charmer’s art is not lacking; the ear is. The man dead in trespasses is not merely uninstructed, so that better argument would move him; he is unresponsive, and stops the ear against the very sweetness that would save. Persuasion alone cannot raise him. Nothing short of effectual grace — the sovereign call that gives the ear it commands — will do. And over against that stands the promise: “Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder” (Psa 91:13), which is the ancient word of Gen 3:15 coming true, the Seed of the woman bruising the serpent’s head and setting the heel of His people upon the whole venomous brood.
webster_summary: A venomous serpent or viper; in Scripture the emblem of poison hidden in the path, and of the ear that will not hear.
webster_full: ADDER, a venomous serpent or viper of the smaller kind.
From the Saxon naedre, a serpent; the n was lost into the article.
Rendering several Hebrew words for venomous snakes of different sorts.
Figuratively, secret malice: “adders’ poison is under their lips” (Psa 140:3).
Figuratively, the sting hidden at the bottom of pleasure (Pro 23:32).
scriptures: Psa 58:4
Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear;
Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah.
corruption_summary: The deaf adder is made an argument for better technique, as though the unconverted needed only a wiser charmer rather than a new ear.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse of Psa 58:4 is to read the deaf adder as a challenge to the charmer’s skill. If the method were sharpened, the music improved, the appeal made warmer or the argument tighter, then surely the ear would open. Whole systems of persuasion have been built on that assumption, and they mistake the psalm exactly backwards. The psalm does not fault the charming; it says the charming was done never so wisely and the ear was stopped anyway. The defect is not in the sound but in the hearer. Man by nature is not a neutral party weighing evidence; he is a stopped ear, and stops it himself, willingly, against the sweetest voice in the world.

Recover the doctrine and the labour is not abandoned but relocated. The charmer still charms — preaching remains the appointed means, and no man is excused from pleading with sinners as though their souls hung on the pleading, for they do. But the preacher no longer preaches as a man with a technique; he preaches as a man begging God to give the ear he is speaking into. Effectual calling is not preaching made more effective; it is the Spirit doing sovereignly what no eloquence can do, opening what was shut. And that is why Psa 91:13 belongs beside Psa 58:4. The adder is not negotiated with. It is trodden down, by the Seed of the woman promised in Gen 3:15, whose heel is bruised and whose foot is on the serpent’s head.
roots_summary: A venomous serpent of the path; in the Psalms the deaf ear of the wicked and the head beneath the believer’s heel.
roots_lines: Adder — Saxon naedre, a serpent; the n worn away into the article.
Renders shephiphon, pethen, 'akshub, and tsiph'oni — venomous snakes of several sorts.
Gen 49:17: an adder in the path that bites the heels and fells the rider.
Psa 58:4: the deaf adder stops her ear against the wisest charming — depravity, not ignorance.
Psa 91:13: the adder trodden under foot, answering the promise of Gen 3:15.
usage: A small enemy in the dust may bring down a great rider (Gen 49:17).
The sting is at the last, not at the first — that is the adder in the cup (Pro 23:32).
The deaf adder needs a new ear, not a better charmer.

etymology: From the Latin leopardus, compounded of leo, a lion, and pardus, a panther, from the old notion that the beast was a cross of the two; rendering the Hebrew namer, a spotted beast of prey, the swift and dappled hunter of the hills of Canaan.
biblical_def: The leopard is the spotted beast of prey, swift, silent and marked for life. Scripture names it for three things: its speed, its lying in wait, and above all its spots. Habakkuk sets the Chaldean cavalry beside it — horses “swifter than the leopards” (Hab 1:8); Daniel sees the third kingdom as a leopard with four wings and four heads, dominion given to it (Dan 7:6), speed itself made an empire. But the verse that carries the doctrine is Jeremiah’s: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23). The prophet is not moralising. He is stating an impossibility and drawing a conclusion from it. A man habituated in sin can no more reform himself than the beast can wash out its markings, for the marking is not on him but in him. This is the bondage of the will in a single image: the sinner does exactly what he wants, and what he wants is the trouble. Nothing but a new nature will serve, which is why regeneration is a birth and not a resolution. And Scripture will not leave the leopard under the curse. In the kingdom of the Branch, “the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa 11:6) — the spots unchanged, the ferocity gone, because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD.
webster_summary: A fierce spotted beast of prey; in Scripture the emblem of swiftness in judgment and of a nature that cannot change itself.
webster_full: LEOPARD, a rapacious quadruped of the cat kind, with a spotted skin.
From the Latin leo, a lion, and pardus, a panther.
Renders the Hebrew namer, the dappled hunter of the hills.
Proverbial for what cannot be altered: “or the leopard his spots” (Jer 13:23).
A figure of swift conquest in prophecy (Dan 7:6; Hab 1:8).
scriptures: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
Isa 11:6
The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
Jer 5:6

Wherefore a lion out of the forest shall slay them, and a wolf of the evenings shall spoil them, a leopard shall watch over their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces: because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.
Hab 1:8

Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat.
corruption_summary: Jer 13:23 is quoted as a shrug — people never change — when the verse is a diagnosis whose only cure is the new birth.
corruption_paragraphs: The leopard’s spots have become a proverb of fatalism. A man is written off, a marriage abandoned, a wayward son given up, and the verse is quoted over the wreckage as though Jeremiah had taught that human nature is fixed and that is the end of the matter. That is half the verse and none of its purpose. Jeremiah is preaching to a people who supposed a little reform would restore them, and he takes away the ladder: you who are accustomed to do evil can no more do good by resolving to than the beast can rub off its markings. The point of an impossibility in Scripture is never resignation. It is to drive the hearer off his own resources and onto God, who does impossible things.

So the verse that seems to close the door is the very one that names where the door is. If the spots cannot be changed from without, the creature must be changed from within — and that is precisely what the Lord promises through the same prophet, a new heart and His law written on the inward parts, and through Ezekiel a heart of flesh for a heart of stone, and through our Lord to Nicodemus a birth from above. Regeneration is not the sinner scrubbing at his skin; it is God giving him a new nature, out of which new doing comes. Isa 11:6 is the picture of the end of it: the leopard still spotted, lying down beside the kid, its whole ferocity taken away by the King who reigns.
roots_summary: The spotted hunter — swift in prophecy, and the standing emblem of a nature no man can alter in himself.
roots_lines: Leopard — Latin leopardus, from leo (lion) and pardus (panther).
Hebrew namer, a spotted beast of prey known in the hills of Canaan.
Jer 13:23 makes the unchangeable spots the figure of habituated sin.
Dan 7:6 and Hab 1:8 use the leopard for the speed of conquering empires; Jer 5:6 for judgment lying in wait.
Isa 11:6 sets the leopard beside the kid in the peace of Messiah’s reign.
usage: The spots are not paint on the beast; they are the beast — and so is sin in the sinner.
Quote Jer 13:23 to end an argument and you have used it against its own purpose.
The leopard of Isa 11:6 keeps its spots and loses its ferocity: grace changes the heart, not the species.

etymology: From the Saxon moththe, a small nocturnal insect whose larva feeds upon wool and cloth; rendering the Hebrew 'ash, the fretting insect of the garment, and the Greek ses, used by our Lord in the Sermon on the Mount.
biblical_def: The moth is the small insect whose larva eats wool, and in Scripture it is the standing emblem of decay working quietly from within. Its work is not violent; nobody hears a moth. The garment is folded away, apparently safe, and comes out ruined. So Job says of frail man that he “consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten” (Job 13:28), and Isaiah says of the accusers of the Servant that “they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up” (Isa 50:9) — the whole apparatus of opposition quietly consumed while the Servant stands justified. Hosea says something more solemn still: “I will be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness” (Hos 5:12). God Himself can be the slow decay in a nation’s cloth, a judgment that does not thunder but eats. Our Lord takes the same image and makes it the argument of the Christian’s whole treasury: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:19), but lay up treasure in heaven, “where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). The reasoning is not that earthly goods are wicked but that they are perishable, and a wise man does not build where the builders are moth and rust. Where the treasure is, there the heart follows; the moth is God’s standing witness that the heart must go somewhere higher.
webster_summary: A small insect whose larva devours cloth; the biblical emblem of quiet, unstoppable decay against which heavenly treasure is laid up.
webster_full: MOTH, a small nocturnal insect whose larva eats and destroys wool and cloth.
From the Saxon moththe; kindred with the Dutch mot.
Renders the Hebrew 'ash and the Greek ses.
Figuratively, anything that secretly and gradually consumes.
Used by our Lord for the perishableness of all earthly treasure (Mat 6:19).
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
And he, as a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten.
Isa 50:9
Behold, the Lord GOD will help me; who is he that shall condemn me? lo, they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up.
corruption_summary: The moth is answered with better storage — insurance, diversification, permanence purchased — when our Lord named it to move the treasure, not to protect it.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest evasion of Mat 6:19 is to hear it as a problem of security rather than of location. Moth and rust corrupt, therefore build a better vault: preserve, insure, hedge, endow, and the decay is defeated. Every age has its version of the strategy and every age discovers the same thing, that the moth is patient and the vault is not eternal. Our Lord did not say earthly treasure was insufficiently guarded. He said it was in the wrong place. The whole force of the command falls on the word where. There is a country in which nothing eats, and He is telling His disciples to bank there.

The remedy is not asceticism, which is only another way of making earthly goods the centre of attention. Scripture commends provision for one’s house, honest labour, the inheritance a good man leaves to his children’s children. But it treats every one of those as a stewardship passing through the hand, not a treasure resting in the heart — for the heart follows the treasure, and a heart lodged among moth-eaten things will be moth-eaten too. Laying up treasure in heaven is done here, in mercy shewn, in the poor relieved, in the gospel sent, in a life spent for Christ. What is given away is the only part of an estate the moth cannot reach.
roots_summary: The cloth-eating insect — quiet decay in a garment, and the measure of everything laid up on earth.
roots_lines: Moth — Saxon moththe, the insect whose larva devours wool.
Hebrew 'ash; Greek ses in the words of our Lord.
Job 13:28 makes it the figure of man’s frailty, consumed like a moth-eaten garment.
Isa 50:9 turns it on the Servant’s accusers — they wax old and the moth eats them up.
Hos 5:12: the LORD Himself as a moth to Ephraim — judgment that eats rather than thunders.
usage: Nobody hears a moth — which is exactly why it is the emblem of decay.
The command of Mat 6:19 is about where, not about how well the vault is built.
What is given away is the only part of an estate the moth cannot reach.

etymology: From the Saxon wyrm, a creeping thing or serpent; in the Authorized Version chiefly the Hebrew rimmah, the maggot of corruption, and tola'ath, the crimson grub, together with the Greek skolex in our Lord’s word upon Gehenna.
biblical_def: The worm in Scripture is the creature of corruption, and it carries five distinct weights. First, it is the judgment on hoarding: manna kept overnight against the plain word of God “bred worms, and stank” (Exo 16:20), so that daily bread must be daily received and stored providence is no providence at all. Second, it is the emblem of the body’s dissolution — and there Job plants the great confession, that “though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God” (Job 19:26). The worm gets the body; it does not keep it. The resurrection is bodily or it is nothing. Third, it is the word of Christ’s abasement on the cross, “I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Psa 22:6) — the Son of God brought to the lowest name a creature has. Fourth, it is the LORD’s tender address to His helpless people: “Fear not, thou worm Jacob… I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 41:14). The name is not withdrawn; the help is added to it. Fifth and most solemn, it is the worm that does not die. Isaiah ends his prophecy with it (Isa 66:24) and our Lord repeats it three times over Gehenna: “Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched” (Mar 9:48). The punishment of the impenitent is conscious and it is everlasting.
webster_summary: A small creeping animal; in Scripture the maggot of corruption, the figure of abasement, and the undying worm of the lost.
webster_full: WORM, a small creeping animal without feet, of many kinds.
From the Saxon wyrm, a creeping thing or serpent.
Renders the Hebrew rimmah (the maggot) and tola'ath (the crimson grub).
Figuratively, a person of the meanest condition: “thou worm Jacob” (Isa 41:14).
Figuratively, that which gnaws and torments without ceasing (Mar 9:48).
scriptures: Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.
And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:
Psa 22:6
But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people.
Mar 9:48
Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.
corruption_summary: Annihilationism attempts to put out the worm that our Lord said does not die, and universalism empties the sentence altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord said three times in one chapter that in Gehenna “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” Annihilationism — the doctrine that the lost are finally extinguished rather than punished for ever — must therefore make the undying worm a figure for a fire that finishes its work and goes out. But a worm that dies is precisely what the text denies, and Isaiah, from whom the words are taken, sets the sight before the redeemed as perpetual, not as a scene that empties. Universalism goes further and cancels the sentence outright, usually by the plea that a God of love would not allow such an end. That plea puts a human sentiment above the plain words of the Judge, who is Himself the meekest and most loving Person who ever spoke, and who spoke of hell more than any other in Scripture. Eternal conscious punishment is not a doctrine the church invented against the tenderness of Christ; it is a doctrine the church received from His own lips.

The recovery is to let the worm say all five of the things Scripture makes it say, and not one alone. It says do not hoard, for the manna bred worms (Exo 16:20) and God feeds His people by the day. It says the grave is not the last word, for after the skin is destroyed the same man in his own flesh shall see God (Job 19:26). It says the Lord of glory took the name of a worm and no man (Psa 22:6) so that worms might be made sons. It says the LORD calls His weak people worms and in the same breath calls Himself their redeemer (Isa 41:14). And it says there is a worm that never dies. To preach the fifth without the other four makes a man harsh; to preach the four and hide the fifth makes him unfaithful. Preach all five and you have the doctrine of Christ.
roots_summary: The creature of corruption — in the manna, in the grave, on the cross, in the LORD’s tender name for His people, and undying in Gehenna.
roots_lines: Worm — Saxon wyrm, a creeping thing; Hebrew rimmah and tola'ath; Greek skolex.
Exo 16:20: hoarded manna bred worms — the doctrine of daily dependence.
Job 19:26: worms destroy the body, yet in his flesh he shall see God.
Psa 22:6 and Isa 41:14: the name of abasement, borne by Christ and spoken tenderly over Jacob.
Mar 9:48, from Isa 66:24: the worm that dieth not — punishment conscious and everlasting.
usage: Manna kept overnight bred worms: God gives bread daily, and will not be stored against.
The worm destroys the body and does not keep it — Job 19:26 is a resurrection text.
“Thou worm Jacob” and “thy redeemer” stand in the same verse; the LORD does not flatter what He saves.

etymology: From the Saxon lus, plural lys, a small wingless insect infesting the skin of men and beasts; rendering the Hebrew kinnim, the swarming vermin of the third plague, raised out of the dust of Egypt at the stroke of Aaron’s rod.
biblical_def: The lice are the vermin of the third plague upon Egypt, and their importance is out of all proportion to their size. The LORD commanded Moses, “Say unto Aaron, Stretch out thy rod, and smite the dust of the land, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt” (Exo 8:16), and the dust of the earth became lice in man and in beast throughout the whole land (Exo 8:17). Egypt was a nation of priests who prized ritual cleanness, shaving the body, washing continually; the plague fell precisely on that. But the decisive thing is what happened next. The magicians, who had matched the rod turned to a serpent and the water turned to blood and the frogs brought up from the river, tried this and failed: “the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not” (Exo 8:18). And these men, the very defenders of Pharaoh’s religion, said to their king, “This is the finger of God” (Exo 8:19). It is the confession of the opposition. Imitation runs out; creation does not. The magicians could counterfeit a sign; they could not make life out of dust, because that is the Creator’s own act, and the dust of Genesis 2 answers here. Yet Pharaoh’s heart was hardened and he hearkened not, as the LORD had said — proof enough that evidence alone converts no one.
webster_summary: Small wingless insects infesting the skin; in Scripture the third plague of Egypt, at which the magicians confessed the finger of God.
webster_full: LICE, the plural of louse, a small wingless insect infesting the skin of animals.
From the Saxon lus, plural lys.
Renders the Hebrew kinnim, the vermin of the third Egyptian plague.
Raised out of the dust of the land at the stroke of Aaron’s rod (Exo 8:16-17).
The plague at which the magicians’ enchantments failed (Exo 8:18).
scriptures: Exo 8:16
And the LORD said unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch out thy rod, and smite the dust of the land, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
Exo 8:17

And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
Exo 8:18
And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not: so there were lice upon man, and upon beast.
Exo 8:19
Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said.
corruption_summary: The plagues are re-told as a chain of ordinary ecological events, which empties them of the one thing the text says they were — the finger of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern retelling makes the ten plagues a natural sequence: a red algal bloom fouls the Nile, the frogs flee the water, the frogs die, the insects breed on the carcases, the flies carry murrain to the cattle, and so on down the chain. The account is offered as a defence of the narrative, and it is nothing of the kind. It concedes the historical-critical premise that the miraculous is the one explanation not permitted, and it fails on its own terms at Exo 8:18, where the magicians — who had reproduced the earlier signs by their enchantments — cannot reproduce this one. If a natural chain were producing the vermin, the men of Egypt would have had no need to reproduce anything; the vermin would simply have come. Their failure, and their confession, are the text’s own commentary. The plagues are not folklore, not legendary material, and not a weather report. They are ten precise blows against the gods of Egypt, and the LORD says so Himself.

Recovering the plague as a plague recovers the doctrine bound up in it. The finger of God is the phrase Scripture uses for what only God does — the tables of the law were written with it, and our Lord cast out devils by it. Here it names the boundary between counterfeit and creation. Satan and his servants can mimic; they cannot make. And the second half of Exo 8:19 is as important as the first: the confession was made, and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened anyway. A man may be handed unanswerable evidence by his own advisers and remain unmoved, which is why the new birth is a necessity and not an improvement. Evidence convinces the mind it finds; only grace gives the heart that will bow.
roots_summary: The vermin of the third plague, raised from the dust, at which Egypt’s magicians confessed the finger of God.
roots_lines: Lice — Saxon lus / lys; Hebrew kinnim, swarming vermin.
Exo 8:16-17: the dust of the land becomes lice throughout all Egypt at Aaron’s rod.
The dust of Gen 2:7 answers here — only the Creator makes life out of dust.
Exo 8:18: the magicians attempt it by enchantments and cannot.
Exo 8:19: “This is the finger of God” — and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened still.
usage: The third plague is where imitation ran out and Egypt’s own priests said so.
Counterfeit can copy a sign; it cannot make a creature from the dust.
Pharaoh had the evidence from his own advisers and hardened his heart against it.

etymology: From the Saxon frogga, an amphibious creature of the marsh; rendering the Hebrew tsephardea', the frog of the Nile, and the Greek batrachos in the vision of the Apocalypse.
biblical_def: The frogs are the second plague of Egypt and, at the end of the Bible, the likeness of three unclean spirits. The LORD warned Pharaoh, “if thou refuse to let them go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs” (Exo 8:2), and when Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters “the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt” (Exo 8:6). The psalm remembers where they went: “their land brought forth frogs in abundance, in the chambers of their kings” (Psa 105:30). Nothing was exempt, not the bedchamber of Pharaoh himself. The stroke fell on Egypt’s religion as well as its comfort, for the frog was a sacred creature of the Nile, emblem of the goddess of fruitfulness; the LORD gave Egypt its deity in such quantity that it became a torment. And He gave Moses the sign of His mastery in the timing: Pharaoh himself named the hour, and “the LORD did according to the word of Moses; and the frogs died out of the houses” (Exo 8:13). A god that can be summoned by an Egyptian magician is no god; a God who removes the plague at an appointed minute is the Lord of it. The image returns in Rev 16:13, where John sees “three unclean spirits like frogs” issuing from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — lying words swarming out of the mouth, croaking in every chamber, gathering the kings of the earth to the battle of the great day.
webster_summary: Amphibious creatures of the marsh; the second plague of Egypt, and in the Apocalypse the likeness of unclean spirits of deceit.
webster_full: FROG, an amphibious animal of the marsh, remarkable for leaping and for its croaking.
From the Saxon frogga.
Renders the Hebrew tsephardea' and the Greek batrachos.
The second of the ten plagues upon Egypt (Exo 8:2-14).
In Rev 16:13, the likeness under which three unclean spirits are seen.
scriptures: Exo 8:2
And if thou refuse to let them go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs:
Exo 8:6
And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt.
Their land brought forth frogs in abundance, in the chambers of their kings.
And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet.
corruption_summary: The second plague is dissolved into a natural chain of river events, and the frogs of Rev 16:13 are treated as scenery rather than as lying doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The frogs are the hinge of the naturalising retelling of the Exodus: a fouled Nile drives the frogs ashore, the frogs die, and the rest of the plagues follow as consequences. It is presented as respect for the text and it is a quiet denial of it, for the narrative does not describe frogs fleeing a river — it describes frogs coming up at the stretching out of a rod, filling the ovens and the kneadingtroughs and the bedchamber of the king, and dying at an hour Pharaoh himself appointed (Exo 8:9-13). A natural chain has no appointments. The plagues are neither folklore nor mythological elements imported into the record; they are history, ten deliberate strokes against Egypt’s gods, and the frog — sacred to Egypt — was chosen with the same precision as every other.

The second corruption is to read Rev 16:13 as mere grotesque imagery. John was shown something exact. The unclean spirits are like frogs, and they come out of the mouth: the emblem is croaking, ceaseless, everywhere at once, filling every chamber, impossible to shut out. That is the character of the world’s deceiving doctrine at the end — not chiefly violent but vocal, multiplying faster than it can be answered, and issuing from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet, which is to say from Satan, from political power, and from corrupted religion. The believer’s defence is not a louder croak but the word of God, and the blessing set in the very next verse upon the man who watches and keeps his garments.
roots_summary: The second plague of Egypt, and the emblem in the Apocalypse of unclean spirits issuing from the mouth.
roots_lines: Frog — Saxon frogga; Hebrew tsephardea'; Greek batrachos.
Exo 8:2-6: frogs cover the land of Egypt at the stretching out of Aaron’s hand.
Psa 105:30: they reach the chambers of the kings — no rank exempted.
Exo 8:13: they die at the hour Pharaoh named — the LORD masters the plague He sent.
Rev 16:13: three unclean spirits like frogs out of the mouths of dragon, beast and false prophet.
usage: Egypt’s sacred frog was given to Egypt in such abundance that it became a torment.
The frogs died at the hour Pharaoh named — that timing is the whole argument.
Frogs out of the mouth: the end-time deception is vocal, ceaseless, and everywhere.

etymology: A compound of English formation, grass and hopper, the leaping insect of the field; in the Authorized Version rendering the Hebrew chagab and kindred words for the locust kind, used chiefly for smallness and for multitude.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version the grasshopper stands for two things which look opposite and are not: littleness and swarming multitude. Midian came up against Israel “as grasshoppers for multitude” (Jdg 6:5), and Nahum mocks the officers of Nineveh as “great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away” (Nah 3:17) — a swarm that looks like an army until the light comes. But the two great uses are set deliberately against each other. At Kadesh the ten spies came back from the land and reported, “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Num 13:33). That is unbelief’s arithmetic: the man measures himself against the giant, finds himself an insect, and calls the sum realism. It is nothing of the kind. He has left out God, who had promised the land, and left out that Caleb and Joshua stood in the same valley, saw the same men, and said the LORD would bring them in. Isaiah supplies the true scale: “It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers” (Isa 40:22). Before the enthroned LORD it is not Israel only but the giants, the nations and the princes of the earth who are the insects. Measured against Anak, a man is a grasshopper; measured against God, so is Anak. Faith uses the second measurement.
webster_summary: A leaping insect of the field; in Scripture the emblem both of vast multitude and of utter smallness before God.
webster_full: GRASSHOPPER, an insect of the field that leaps and chirps, of the locust kind.
Compounded of grass and hopper, from its leaping in the grass.
Renders the Hebrew chagab and related words for the locust family.
Used for innumerable multitude: “as grasshoppers for multitude” (Jdg 6:5).
Used for insignificance before God (Isa 40:22) and before men (Num 13:33).
scriptures: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
Jdg 6:5
For they came up with their cattle and their tents, and they came as grasshoppers for multitude; for both they and their camels were without number: and they entered into the land to destroy it.
Nah 3:17

Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.
corruption_summary: The spies’ grasshopper report is treated as a problem of self-image, to be cured by thinking better of oneself — when the fault was thinking too little of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Num 13:33 has been made a text about self-esteem. The spies felt small, the sermon runs, and their smallness of feeling lost them the land; therefore see yourself as more than a grasshopper. But Isa 40:22 says the inhabitants of the earth are as grasshoppers, and says it as settled truth. The spies’ error was not that they estimated themselves too low; it was that they took their own sight as the measure of reality — “in our own sight” is the confession in the verse itself — and never put the promise of God into the sum at all. A man who thinks better of himself and still leaves God out has changed nothing but the size of the insect.

The cure is a bigger God, not a bigger self, and the ten spies had every material for it. They had seen the Nile turned to blood, the sea divided, the manna each morning, the pillar by night. Caleb and Joshua looked at the same walls and the same sons of Anak and reported that the LORD would bring the people in, and their confidence was not in the arm of Israel but in the word already given. That is faith’s arithmetic: not the denial that the giants are giants, but the insistence that God is God. Israel wandered forty years because it measured by self, and the two men who measured by the promise were the only two of that generation who went in.
roots_summary: The leaping insect of the field — the measure of unbelief at Kadesh and of the nations before the enthroned LORD.
roots_lines: Grasshopper — English grass + hopper; Hebrew chagab and kindred locust words.
Jdg 6:5: Midian comes up “as grasshoppers for multitude”.
Num 13:33: the ten spies measure themselves by the giants and report insects.
Isa 40:22: before the LORD enthroned, the inhabitants of the earth are the grasshoppers.
Nah 3:17: Nineveh’s captains a swarm that flees when the sun arises.
usage: “In our own sight” is the whole error of Num 13:33 — own sight, not God’s promise.
Measured against Anak a man is a grasshopper; measured against God, so is Anak.
Caleb and Joshua saw the same giants and gave the other report.

etymology: From the Saxon ra or raa, the small deer of the woods; rendering the Hebrew tsebi and its feminine tsebiyyah, the gazelle — a clean beast permitted for food (Deu 12:15), proverbial for swiftness, beauty, and shyness.
biblical_def: The roe is the gazelle of the hills, the swiftest and most timid of the clean beasts, and Scripture uses it for three things: speed, beauty, and a shyness that must not be startled. It is the standing figure for a man’s deliverance — “deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter” (Pro 6:5), where the counsel to a man who has struck hands in suretiship is not to negotiate but to get out, and quickly. It measures the speed of warriors: Asahel the son of Zeruiah was as light of foot as a wild roe (2Sa 2:18), and the Gadites who came to David in the hold were as swift as the roes upon the mountains (1Ch 12:8) — a swiftness that killed Asahel, since he would not turn aside from Abner. But the Song of Solomon makes the roe its own. The Bride charges the daughters of Jerusalem “by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Son 2:7), and the oath is sworn by the shyest creatures in the country because the thing to be guarded is that shy: love has its hour, and to force the hour is to lose the thing. Of the Bridegroom she says, “My beloved is like a roe or a young hart” (Son 2:9), and the book closes with her calling him to come like a roe upon the mountains of spices (Son 8:14) — swift, eager, and coming at his own appointed time.
webster_summary: Small swift deer, the gazelles of the hills; in Scripture emblems of speed, beauty, and a love not to be forced before its hour.
webster_full: ROE, a species of small and very swift deer, remarkable for beauty and timidity.
From the Saxon ra; the Hebrew tsebi, the gazelle.
A clean beast, permitted to Israel for food (Deu 12:15; Deu 14:5).
Proverbial for swiftness of foot in warriors (2Sa 2:18; 1Ch 12:8).
In the Song of Solomon, the emblem of the Beloved and of love unforced (Son 2:7-9).
scriptures: Son 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
Son 2:9
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.
Son 8:14
Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices.
Pro 6:5
Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.
corruption_summary: The Song’s repeated charge not to stir up love before its hour is the plainest word in Scripture against a culture that treats desire as its own permission.
corruption_paragraphs: Three times the Bride swears the daughters of Jerusalem by the roes and the hinds of the field that they stir not up nor awake love till he please. That charge is now inverted at every level of the culture: desire is treated as self-authorising, the hour is whenever the feeling arrives, and any restraint is named repression. The Song answers with the shyest creature in the country. A roe is not driven; startle it and it is gone. Love in Scripture is covenantal before it is consummated, and the order is not arbitrary — it is the way the thing is made. What is forced open before its hour is not gained early; it is spoiled.

The recovery is a positive one, not a merely restraining one. The Song is in the canon, unabridged, and it is unembarrassed: the Beloved is admired, the Bride speaks her desire plainly, and the whole is set within the covenant of one man and one woman. Chastity in the unmarried and delight in the married are the same doctrine seen at two hours of the same day. And the figure reaches higher still, for the church looks for a Bridegroom who is like a roe upon the mountains — swift, and coming at the hour His Father has appointed. “Make haste, my beloved” is the last word of the book, and it is very near the last word of the Bible.
roots_summary: The gazelle of the hills — swift, beautiful, easily startled, and the Song’s emblem of love that keeps its hour.
roots_lines: Roe — Saxon ra; Hebrew tsebi / tsebiyyah, the gazelle.
A clean beast, permitted for food in Deu 12:15 and Deu 14:5.
Pro 6:5: escape suretiship as a roe from the hand of the hunter.
2Sa 2:18 and 1Ch 12:8: Asahel and the Gadites swift as roes upon the mountains.
Son 2:7: the daughters of Jerusalem charged by the roes not to awake love till he please.
usage: The oath is sworn by the shyest creature in the country, because the thing guarded is that shy.
Asahel’s roe-swiftness carried him to Abner’s spear — speed without discretion is no gift.
“Till he please” — love has an hour, and forcing the hour spoils the love.

etymology: From the Saxon nest, the bed or habitation a bird builds for her young; rendering the Hebrew qen, a nest or brood, and the Greek kataskenosis, a lodging-place, in the words of our Lord concerning the birds of the air.
biblical_def: The nest in Scripture is the small home a creature makes, and God takes notice of it. The law of Deu 22:6 forbids taking the mother bird with the young: “thou shalt not take the dam with the young” — a mercy statute so small that it proves the point of all the rest, that the God who governs empires legislates about a bird’s nest in a hedge. The psalmist, shut out from the courts of the LORD, envies the smallest tenant there: “Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts” (Psa 84:3). Even a sparrow has a place at those altars, and that is the ground of the pilgrim’s hope. Solomon warns of the man who leaves his post as “a bird that wandereth from her nest” (Pro 27:8), and the prophets turn the nest against the proud, telling Edom that though he set his nest among the stars he would be brought down (Oba 1:4). But the word gets its weight from our Lord: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Mat 8:20). He who made every nest and numbered every sparrow was in this world without one. The homelessness is voluntary: He had no place to lay His head that His people might have a house not made with hands.
webster_summary: The bed or habitation a bird builds for her young; guarded by God’s law, found even at His altars, and denied to the Son of man.
webster_full: NEST, the place or bed formed by a bird for incubation and rearing her young.
From the Saxon nest; Hebrew qen; Greek kataskenosis, a lodging.
Protected by the mercy law of Deu 22:6, which spares the dam.
Figuratively, a man’s settled place, from which it is dangerous to wander (Pro 27:8).
Figuratively, a proud security thought unreachable (Oba 1:4; Jer 49:16).
scriptures: Deu 22:6

If a bird's nest chance to be before thee in the way in any tree, or on the ground, whether they be young ones, or eggs, and the dam sitting upon the young, or upon the eggs, thou shalt not take the dam with the young:
Psa 84:3
Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God.
Mat 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Pro 27:8
As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place.
corruption_summary: Mat 8:20 is turned into a sentimental picture of a homeless teacher, and Deu 22:6 into a mere conservation rule — both stripped of the doctrine in them.
corruption_paragraphs: “The Son of man hath not where to lay his head” is quoted as pathos, a wistful line about a wandering teacher. It is nothing so soft. It is spoken to a scribe who had just volunteered to follow Him anywhere, and it is a demand that the man count the cost before he speaks again. And beneath the demand lies the deeper thing: the poverty is voluntary. He who fitted every hedge with a nest and clothed the lilies chose to own nothing, was born in a borrowed stable and buried in a borrowed tomb, and did it as the whole tenor of a life laid down. Take the pathos and leave the substitution, and the verse has been emptied.

Deu 22:6 suffers the opposite reduction, being filed away as an early conservation measure. It is a mercy statute, and its logic runs the other way: take the young if you have need, but do not take the mother with them — do not, in gratifying a present appetite, destroy the source of tomorrow’s provision, and do not harden yourself against the creature’s helplessness while she sits. Our Lord builds on exactly that scale when He says two sparrows are sold for a farthing and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. The God who numbers the hairs of a man’s head is the God who wrote a law about a bird’s nest, and the smallness of the law is the size of the comfort.
roots_summary: The bird’s home — protected by law, found at God’s altars, denied to the Son of man.
roots_lines: Nest — Saxon nest; Hebrew qen; Greek kataskenosis, a lodging-place.
Deu 22:6: the dam is not to be taken with the young — a mercy statute of the smallest scale.
Psa 84:3: the sparrow and the swallow find a nest at the altars of the LORD of hosts.
Pro 27:8: the man who wanders from his place is a bird gone from her nest.
Mat 8:20: the birds have nests; the Son of man had nowhere to lay His head.
usage: God legislates about a bird’s nest — the smallness of the law is the size of the comfort.
The sparrow has a place at His altars, and so may the pilgrim (Psa 84:3).
Mat 8:20 is not pathos; it is a bill handed to a volunteer before he enlists.

etymology: From the Saxon colt, the young of the horse or ass kind; rendering the Hebrew 'ayir, a young male ass, and the Greek polos, a foal — the beast on which the King of Zion rode into His city.
biblical_def: The colt is the young ass, and Scripture makes it the mount of the promised King. The blessing of Judah in Gen 49:11 binds “his ass’s colt unto the choice vine” — an image of such abundance that a man may tether a beast where the fruit grows — and Zechariah takes up the same line: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion… behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9). Every word there is deliberate. He is just; He has salvation; and He is lowly. A conqueror came on a war-horse. The King of Zion came on the colt of a working beast, and the humility is not a lapse from the majesty but the form the majesty took. Matthew records the fulfilment in the very words of the prophet (Mat 21:5), and John after Him (Joh 12:15). Two further details preach. The colt was one “whereon never man sat” (Luk 19:30; Mar 11:2) — what is consecrated to God must be unused by common service — and an unbroken colt carried Him quietly through a shouting crowd, which the creation does for its Maker. And He came riding on a borrowed beast, loosed at His word, to a city that would cry Hosanna on the Sunday and Crucify on the Friday. The King came lowly, and was received exactly as lowly kings are.
webster_summary: The young of the horse or ass; in prophecy and fulfilment the beast on which the King of Zion rode lowly into His city.
webster_full: COLT, the young of the horse or of the ass kind.
From the Saxon colt; Hebrew 'ayir; Greek polos, a foal.
Bound to the choice vine in the blessing of Judah (Gen 49:11).
Foretold as the mount of the coming King in Zec 9:9.
Fulfilled in the entry into Jerusalem (Mat 21:5; Joh 12:15).
scriptures: Binding his foal unto the vine, and his ass's colt unto the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes:
Zec 9:9

Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
Mat 21:5
Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass.
Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt.
corruption_summary: The lowly colt is made a lesson in humble leadership technique, and the triumphal entry a piece of political theatre, when it is a prophecy kept to the letter.
corruption_paragraphs: Two reductions run alongside each other. The first turns Zec 9:9 into a management principle: the King rode a donkey, therefore leaders should be approachable. The second, more corrosive, treats the entry as staged street theatre, a deliberate anti-imperial gesture crafted by a religious teacher for effect. Both leave out the one thing the Gospels insist on, that this was prophecy fulfilled — written five hundred years before by Zechariah, and before that pointed at in the blessing of Judah, and carried out to the letter down to the colt whereon never man sat. Matthew does not present it as a gesture. He quotes the prophet, and says it was done that it might be fulfilled.

The lowliness is therefore doctrine, not style. He is just, and He has salvation, and He is lowly, all in one verse; the humility of the colt does not qualify the kingship, it displays the kind of King He is — one who comes to bear a cross before He takes a crown. And it is deliberately not the whole picture, for the same Christ is seen in Rev 19 upon a white horse, in righteousness judging and making war. The first coming was on a colt; the second will not be. To take the lowliness of the entry as the whole of His character is to mistake the hour for the Person.
roots_summary: The young ass — bound to the choice vine in Judah’s blessing, and the mount of the King who came lowly to Zion.
roots_lines: Colt — Saxon colt; Hebrew 'ayir, a young ass; Greek polos, a foal.
Gen 49:11 binds the ass’s colt to the choice vine in the blessing of Judah.
Zec 9:9 foretells the King, just, having salvation, and lowly, upon a colt.
Mat 21:5 and Joh 12:15 record the fulfilment at the entry into Jerusalem.
Luk 19:30 and Mar 11:2: a colt whereon never man sat — consecrated, and quiet under its Maker.
usage: A conqueror came on a war-horse; the King of Zion came on a colt.
“Whereon never man sat” — what is consecrated to God is kept from common use.
The first coming was on a colt; the second is on a white horse.
